To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the relationship between well-being measures and income is linear-log; 2) the linear-log relationship holds across countries, across income groups within countries and over time; 3) the linear-log coefficient is the same across countries; and 4) the linear-log relation holds across a range of well-being measures.

(a) the relationship between subjective well-being and income appears roughly linear-log, (b) the relationship does not become flatter as income rises, (c) the relationship between income and subjective well-being is similar in poor and rich countries, and (d) the relationship between objective and subjective measures of well-being appears roughly linear-log.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between well-being (or life satisfaction) and income, and in particular, whether this relationship is satiated.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no evidence of a satiation point.
there is no evidence of satiation.
there is a positive and statistically significant relationship between income and well-being.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there is a strong positive correlation between income and well-being and that there is little evidence of diminishing marginal utility of income.
there is no evidence that higher income does not lead to higher subjective well-being.
the relationship between income and happiness is not a U-shaped curve, as some have suggested, but a linear-log curve.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the relationship between income and well-being is not well understood, and that it is important to continue to study it.
there is no reason to think that higher incomes are no longer associated with greater well-being.
there is a strong relationship between income and subjective well-being, and this relationship does not diminish as income rises. © notice
